evidence_items.excerpt: A factor analysis on the belief items revealed a single Non-physicalist Beliefs factor with good internal consistency (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.86). Positive loadings included separate and supernatural realms, a non-natural unifying principle, panpsychism, dualism, and solipsism/idealism; negative loadings included hard materialism, physicalism, and naturalism.
evidence_items.overview: This factor-analysis result defines the main outcome variable used throughout the study. It matters because the reported belief changes are not tied to a single questionnaire item, but to a composite that contrasts non-physicalist positions with hard materialist or naturalist positions. The interpretation remains bounded by the authors’ warning that philosophical labels for items are contestable.
evidence_items.title: Non-Physicalist Factor Structure

evidence_items.excerpt: Pooling scores for the NPB factor, analyses revealed a significant shift away from physicalism at 4 weeks compared with baseline (t(121) = 3.66, p = 0.001, d = 0.33, 95% CI [0.12, 0.39]). These changes were sustained 6 months after the ceremony (t(121) = 5.07, p < 0.0001, d = 0.46, 95% CI [0.22, 0.50]).
evidence_items.overview: The pre-versus-post comparison is the central prospective evidence that psychedelic ceremonies were followed by measurable movement away from hard physicalism. It establishes temporal ordering and durability for the composite non-physicalist belief measure, though the observational ceremony context means it does not by itself fully isolate the pharmacological cause.
evidence_items.title: Prospective Belief Shift

evidence_items.excerpt: For respondents embarking on their first psychedelic experience, significant changes were found at 4 weeks (t(52) = 3.85, p = 0.001, d = 0.53, 95% CI [0.21, 0.66]) and 6 months (t(52) = 5.32, p < 0.0001, d = 0.73, 95% CI [0.36, 0.80]).
evidence_items.overview: The stronger effect sizes among psychedelic-naive participants support the interpretation that the observed shifts are not merely a residue of earlier psychedelic exposure. This evidence is especially relevant to causal interpretation, while still sharing the observational limitations of the ceremony cohort.
evidence_items.title: Naive Participant Effects

evidence_items.excerpt: A significant positive correlation was found between previous psychedelic use and shifts away from the hard-materialism pole of the hard-materialism vs. hard-dualism spectrum at baseline (r = 0.223, p < 0.0001). Figure 2 reports that lifetime psychedelic use was positively correlated with panpsychist views and negatively correlated with hard materialistic views measured at baseline.
evidence_items.overview: The cross-sectional baseline correlation gives convergent evidence that psychedelic exposure and metaphysical orientation vary together even before the prospective ceremony interval. It is not sufficient for causation, but it reinforces the direction of the prospective findings and specifically links past exposure to panpsychist and anti-materialist endorsement.
evidence_items.title: Lifetime Use Correlations

evidence_items.excerpt: The psychedelic ceremony was associated with increases in Fatalistic determinism at 4 weeks versus baseline (t(121) = 2.81, p = 0.012, d = 0.25, 95% CI [0.06, 0.37]); however, this effect did not persist at 6 months. For psychedelic-naive participants, the 6-month effect persisted (t(52) = 2.86, p = 0.012, d = 0.39, 95% CI [0.11, 0.64]).
evidence_items.overview: This result separates fatalism from the more durable non-physicalist belief changes. It shows that psychedelic-associated belief change is not uniform across metaphysical domains and that subgroup history matters: the overall sample shows a temporary fatalism increase, while first-time users show a longer-lasting one.
evidence_items.title: Fatalism Time Course

evidence_items.excerpt: A significant positive correlation was found between shifts away from hard-materialism (the NPB factor) and changes in well-being. The correlation was significant at 4 weeks and at 6 months post-ceremony. Figure 3 states that shifts away from hard materialistic beliefs are associated with increases in well-being.
evidence_items.overview: This figure-level and text-level evidence connects metaphysical belief change to psychological outcome, making the findings relevant beyond abstract belief measurement. The evidence establishes association, not whether non-physicalist belief change causes well-being improvement or whether both reflect a wider therapeutic process.
evidence_items.title: Well-Being Association

evidence_items.excerpt: Path analysis supported a model with excellent fit in which perceived emotional synchrony with other participants—moderated by baseline peer conformity—predicted subsequent changes in the NPB factor. Acute emotional synchrony was itself predicted by trait absorption, gender, age, baseline beliefs, and identity fusion with the ceremony group.
evidence_items.overview: The path model provides a candidate mechanism for belief change in ceremonial settings. It suggests that psychedelic effects operate through social and contextual experience, not only through isolated drug exposure. Because the model is observational, it should be read as mechanistic evidence for plausibility rather than proof of a single causal chain.
evidence_items.title: Emotional Synchrony Pathway

evidence_items.excerpt: In the double-blind randomized trial, a significant drug versus time interaction was observed (F(56) = 3.13, p = 0.041, one-tailed). Shifts away from hard materialism were evident in the psilocybin group only (Z = 2.28, p = 0.02, d = 0.45), while the escitalopram group showed no changes in NPB (Z = 0.24, p = 0.33, d = 0.2).
evidence_items.overview: The controlled-trial evidence is the strongest design element in the paper because it compares psilocybin therapy against an active antidepressant condition. It supports specificity of the belief shift to psilocybin in this depression-treatment sample, though the trial is smaller than the observational survey and differs in population and context.
evidence_items.title: Controlled Psilocybin Comparison

evidence_items.excerpt: Greater shifts away from hard materialistic beliefs were found for patients with a clinically meaningful response to psilocybin therapy, defined as at least 50% reduction in depression scores from baseline to week 6, compared with responders to escitalopram (Z = 1.74, p = 0.041, g = 0.56, 90% CI [− 0.17, 1.26]).
evidence_items.overview: This result links metaphysical belief change to clinically meaningful improvement within the controlled depression study. It complements the ceremony cohort’s well-being association, but it still leaves open whether belief change is a driver, marker, or consequence of clinical response.
evidence_items.title: Responder Belief Shift

A plausible social-experiential pathway makes the causal interpretation more coherent while preserving contextual limits.
The randomized psilocybin comparison independently reproduces the predicted movement away from hard materialism.
Durability at six months is derived from the same non-physicalist belief shift measured prospectively.
Both claims connect movement away from materialism with positive mental-health or clinical-response outcomes.

source.display_title: Psychedelics Shift Beliefs Beyond Hard Materialism

sections.body: The paper’s central argument is that psychedelic use can move people away from hard physicalist or materialist metaphysical positions. This is not framed as a purely philosophical thesis; it is operationalized through questionnaire items and tested before and after psychedelic exposure, then compared with a controlled psilocybin therapy dataset.
sections.heading: Central Argument

sections.body: The main measurement device is a Metaphysical Beliefs Questionnaire whose items are reduced to a Non-physicalist Beliefs factor. The factor’s positive side includes supernatural realms, non-natural unifying principles, panpsychism, dualism, and idealism, while its negative side includes hard materialist and naturalist commitments. This makes the results interpretable as movement along a materialist-to-non-physicalist axis rather than a single-item endorsement change.
sections.heading: Measurement Strategy

sections.body: The ceremony cohort supplies the main temporal evidence: respondents’ non-physicalist scores increase four weeks after psychedelic use and remain elevated at six months. The effect is stronger among psychedelic-naive participants, which supports the possibility that new exposure matters rather than only pre-existing psychedelic-culture affiliation.
sections.heading: Prospective Findings

sections.body: The belief changes are not uniform. Panpsychist, dualist, transcendentalist, and related non-physicalist tendencies show durability, while fatalistic determinism rises more transiently in the overall sample. This distinction matters because it suggests psychedelics may alter several metaphysical domains differently, depending on cultural reinforcement, prior exposure, and interpretive context.
sections.heading: Belief Domains

sections.body: The path model emphasizes social experience during the ceremony. Perceived emotional synchrony predicts later non-physicalist belief change, with peer conformity moderating the pathway and traits such as absorption, age, gender, baseline beliefs, and identity fusion feeding into synchrony. The source therefore treats psychedelic belief change as a drug-context interaction rather than an isolated pharmacological effect.
sections.heading: Mechanism and Context

sections.body: The paper connects metaphysical movement away from hard materialism with better mental-health outcomes. In the ceremony data, such shifts correlate with well-being improvements at four weeks and six months. In the controlled depression trial, psilocybin responders show larger belief shifts than escitalopram responders, raising the possibility that belief flexibility, spiritual interpretation, or related therapeutic processes accompany clinical improvement.
sections.heading: Mental-Health Link

sections.body: The authors stress that the samples are not demographically or culturally neutral and that religious affiliation, environmental susceptibility, and surrounding metaphysical views were not fully measured. These limits temper causal certainty but also sharpen the ethical issue: if psychedelics can catalyze changes in core beliefs, participants and service users may need to be informed of that possibility before exposure.
sections.heading: Limits and Ethics

source_dossier.summary_long: The source investigates a question often asserted in psychedelic culture but rarely tested quantitatively: whether psychedelic experiences alter deep metaphysical commitments. The authors use a large prospective online survey of people planning guided or ceremonial psychedelic experiences, measuring beliefs before the event and again afterward, and they supplement this with data from a randomized controlled depression trial comparing psilocybin therapy with escitalopram. The main construct is a Non-physicalist Beliefs factor built from questionnaire items about supernatural realms, non-natural unifying principles, panpsychism, dualism, idealism, materialism, and naturalism. Across the ceremony sample, scores shift significantly away from hard physicalism at four weeks and remain shifted at six months, with larger effects in psychedelic-naive participants. Fatalistic determinism also rises after ceremonies, but its durability is weaker in the overall sample. The paper further reports that baseline lifetime psychedelic exposure correlates with stronger panpsychist and weaker materialist views, that shifts away from hard materialism correlate with improved well-being, and that a path model identifies perceived emotional synchrony during the ceremony as a mediator of later non-physicalist belief change. The controlled trial adds an important check: psilocybin therapy, but not escitalopram, is associated with movement away from hard materialism at six weeks, and psilocybin responders show greater shifts than escitalopram responders. The authors therefore argue that psychedelic use may causally influence metaphysical beliefs, but they do not treat the causal case as settled. They flag limitations including atypical, largely Western and well-educated samples, missing religious-affiliation and environmental-susceptibility measures, and incomplete measurement of the cultural milieu around ceremonies and therapy. The practical upshot is both scientific and ethical: psychedelic experiences may affect core beliefs, and informed consent in psychedelic services may need to mention that possibility.
source_dossier.summary_short: This Scientific Reports article examines whether psychedelics change metaphysical beliefs. It reports shifts away from hard materialism toward non-physicalist views, supported by a ceremony survey and a smaller psilocybin trial. The findings are linked to emotional synchrony and mental-health improvement but remain context-limited.

summary: Timmermann and colleagues report that psychedelic use is associated with shifts away from hard materialist metaphysical beliefs toward non-physicalist views, with convergent evidence from a prospective ceremony survey and a smaller controlled psilocybin therapy trial. The strongest results concern non-physicalist belief change, persistence to six months, mediation by emotional synchrony, and association with improved well-being or depression response, while publication date metadata could not be resolved from the local record.
